retrieved_context.passage:
ensures you can stay on track with your major-specific classes and labs without delays; Reduce First-Year Stress – College is a big transition. Starting with a strong math foundation can make your first semester feel more manageable and less overwhelming;

Lower the Risk of Academic Notice (in some places this is known as Academic Probation) – Students who come in with a strong Precalculus background have higher GPAs and are less likely to be on Academic Notice in future semesters.

Please note that if you are a PREP-mandated student (meaning participating in PREP is a condition of your admission), you will not be able to take a summer course beyond July 14th

The Chain Reaction: Why Math Controls Your Schedule

Math is the “key” that unlocks your other core requirements. If you are delayed in Calculus, you are effectively “locked out” of the foundational Physics and programming courses that define your first two years.

1. The Physics Barrier

The PHYSICS 5 or 7 series (required for all engineering majors) is heavily calculus-based.

PHYSICS 5A or 7A: These requirements need you to have already completed or be concurrently enrolled in the second semester of Calculus (MATH 52). This means MATH 51 (Calculus 1) needs to be completed before you even start the Physics series.

[ANSWER]
Learning for cloud security and embedded device security would differ significantly in their focus and approach, given the unique characteristics of each domain. For cloud security, students would need to understand the intricacies of cloud infrastructure, including virtualization, containerization, and cloud-native applications. They would also need to be familiar with cloud security services such as Identity and Access Management (IAM), encryption, and security monitoring tools. In contrast, embedded device security would involve understanding the hardware and firmware of devices, as well as the security protocols used in these devices. Students would need to learn about secure boot, secure firmware updates, and the use of hardware security modules (HSMs) to protect against attacks. Both areas require a strong foundation in cybersecurity principles, but the specific technical skills and knowledge needed differ greatly.

Title: Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK Guide), Version 4.0
Source: IEEE Computer Society
URL: https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering
Date accessed: 2026-10-13

Curated source note

The IEEE Computer Society's SWEBOK Guide describes software engineering as more than writing code. It organizes professional software work into knowledge areas that include requirements, architecture, design, construction, testing, maintenance, configuration management, engineering process, models and methods, quality, security, professional practice, economics, and computing foundations.

For Computer Engineering advising, this source helps explain why students should learn software development habits early. Useful habits include reading requirements carefully, designing before coding, using version control, testing and debugging systematically, reviewing code, documenting decisions, thinking about maintainability, and treating security and quality as part of engineering rather than as optional extras.

The source also helps distinguish programming from software engineering. Programming is essential, but professional software engineering also includes working with stakeholders, understanding constraints, selecting designs, managing change, validating behavior, and maintaining systems after initial implementation.

Student-facing guidance: a CENG student who wants backend, frontend, mobile, cloud, AI, or embedded software work should build not only language knowledge but also project structure, testing, Git/GitHub, debugging, design, communication, and teamwork skills. These practices make portfolio projects more credible because they show the student can build software in a professional way.
